answers.primary: A PreToolUse hook registered in settings.json, matching the file-writing tools (Write, Edit, MultiEdit, NotebookEdit) and Bash, that inspects the tool input and returns a deny decision when the resolved target path falls under secrets/. Back it with an explicit deny entry in the permissions block of settings.json so the path is refused at two independent layers rather than one.
answers.rejected_alternative: A prohibition written into CLAUDE.md or a project rules file, rejected because that is instruction text the model reads and can be argued out of, which is precisely the convention compliance says is not good enough.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. The hook process runs before the tool executes and its verdict is applied by Claude Code, not by the model's judgement, so a crafted prompt or the model's own reasoning cannot talk past it.
answers.context_boundary: The hook body runs in a separate OS process with no access to the conversation. Only the serialized tool name and tool input cross into it, and only a decision plus a short reason string crosses back into the transcript, where the model sees that the call was blocked.
answers.lifecycle: Fires on every matching tool call for the whole session, from the moment the settings file is loaded at session start. It stops applying only if the settings entry is removed or the hook script is deleted, and edits to hook config generally require a new session to take effect.
answers.failure_mode: It fails closed on the calls it recognises, but the real risk is matcher coverage rather than bypass: a shell one-liner that cds first, a relative path, a symlink into secrets/, a glob, or a command that pipes the file through cat can dodge a naive string match. Decide deliberately what happens when the hook script itself errors or times out, because a non-blocking exit status there turns the guarantee into a silent fail-open.
answers.version_caveat: Hook configuration and the shape of the PreToolUse decision payload have changed across Claude Code releases (older builds signalled a block by exit status alone, newer ones accept a structured JSON decision on stdout). I cannot state the exact version that introduced the structured form, so the script should be written and tested against the version actually installed.

answers.primary: A skill: a SKILL.md whose frontmatter carries only a name and a tight trigger description, with the 400 ordered steps in the body (or split into reference files the body points at) and the two helper scripts shipped alongside it as executable files invoked by path.
answers.rejected_alternative: Putting the runbook in CLAUDE.md, rejected because CLAUDE.md is loaded into every conversation in the repo, which is exactly the standing token cost the team is objecting to.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model. The harness makes the skill available, but the model decides from the description whether this conversation is a release, so nothing forces the runbook to load or to be followed once loaded.
answers.context_boundary: Only the skill name and description sit in context by default; the body enters the main session's context when the skill is invoked and then stays resident for the rest of that session. The helper scripts never need to enter context at all if they are executed rather than read, which is the main reason to ship them as files.
answers.lifecycle: Triggered when the model matches the description to the user's request, or when the user names it explicitly. It applies from that point to the end of the session; there is no unload, so the once-a-week cost is paid only in release conversations.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory and fails open in both directions. A vague description means the skill never fires during a real release and the model improvises the steps from memory; an over-broad one means it loads during unrelated work and reintroduces the cost. Once loaded, a 400-step ordered procedure is also prone to step skipping, so the body should be structured with explicit checkpoints rather than a flat list.
answers.version_caveat: Agent Skills require a Claude Code version that supports the skills directory and frontmatter loading, and the discovery locations (project .claude/skills, user-level, plugin-bundled) have expanded over releases. I cannot give the exact minimum version from model knowledge alone.

answers.primary: An MCP server for the tracker, configured for the project, exposing narrow tools such as get_ticket, search_tickets and update_ticket. If the tracker speaks OAuth over HTTP, use the remote transport so the server handles the authorization flow and token refresh; otherwise wrap the API in a local stdio server that holds the credential.
answers.rejected_alternative: A skill that shells out to a curl or CLI wrapper, rejected because it puts token handling and refresh into prompt-driven shell commands and gives the model no typed contract for the tracker.
answers.enforcement_owner: Split, but the harness owns the part that matters: it establishes the connection, holds the credential and enforces the tool schema. The model owns the decision of when to call a tool and what to write back, so ticket mutations are model-judgement, not guaranteed.
answers.context_boundary: The server runs as its own process outside the conversation. The tool definitions occupy system-prompt space for the whole session, while only the arguments the model sends and the response body the server returns cross the boundary per call. Credentials stay on the server side and never enter context.
answers.lifecycle: The server is started or connected at session start from the project MCP config and its tools stay available for the session. Authorization must be completed once interactively; expiry mid-session causes calls to fail until re-auth. It stops applying when the config entry is removed or the server is disabled.
answers.failure_mode: Two practical failures. First, tool-description bloat: a chatty server can spend a lot of every context window on schemas, so keep the exposed surface small. Second and more serious, ticket bodies are untrusted third-party text, so instructions embedded in a ticket can be read as directions; treat returned content as data. Auth failures are visible errors rather than silent, so it fails closed on access, but the model choosing not to update a ticket fails open and silently.
answers.version_caveat: OAuth-backed remote MCP servers need a build that supports the HTTP or SSE transport plus the OAuth handshake, and the authorization step cannot be completed in a non-interactive or CI session. Self-hosted servers usually also require registering a client and an allowed redirect URI. I cannot state the exact Claude Code version that added remote OAuth support.

answers.primary: A SessionStart hook configured for the repo that runs a small script (git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD plus a call to the tracker for the current sprint) and returns the result as additional context injected into the new session.
answers.rejected_alternative: CLAUDE.md, rejected because it is static text committed to the repo and cannot pull the branch or sprint list live at the moment the session opens.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. The hook runs unconditionally when a session starts, so no one has to ask and the model cannot decline to gather the information.
answers.context_boundary: The script executes in its own process with no view of the conversation. Only its stdout, as an additional-context block, crosses into the main session's context, where it sits for the whole session as if it had been typed at the top.
answers.lifecycle: Fires once per session start, including on resume or clear depending on how the matcher is configured. It is a one-shot snapshot: nothing refreshes it, so the branch and ticket list it injected go stale the moment someone switches branches or a ticket moves.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open, and usually quietly. If the tracker is unreachable, slow, or the auth token expired, the hook errors or times out and the session simply starts without the context while the model behaves as if it knows the sprint. It also taxes every single session start with network latency, so the script needs a hard timeout and should emit an explicit note when the fetch failed rather than nothing.
answers.version_caveat: The SessionStart event and the structured additional-context output field are later additions to the hook system than PreToolUse; older builds only supported plain stdout injection or no such event at all. I cannot name the introducing version, so verify the event name and output key against the installed build.

answers.primary: A plugin, published through a marketplace the org controls and installed by each repo or each developer. One plugin bundle carries the code-review helper as a skill or command, the lifecycle automations as hooks, and the tracker integration as an MCP server definition, all under a single version number in the plugin manifest.
answers.rejected_alternative: Copying a .claude directory into all 40 repos (or vendoring it as a git submodule), rejected because it gives no version identity and no update path: fixing a hook means opening 40 pull requests.
answers.enforcement_owner: Split by component and this is the point to be explicit about. The harness owns the hooks the plugin ships, so those are guaranteed once installed; the model owns whether the skill and the MCP tools get used. The platform team owns the release, but it does not own whether a consumer actually installs or updates.
answers.context_boundary: Each bundled component keeps its own boundary rather than the plugin having one: hook scripts run outside the conversation, the skill stays out of context until triggered, and the MCP tool schemas sit in the system prompt of every session where the plugin is enabled.
answers.lifecycle: Installed once per consumer from the marketplace, loaded at session start, and updated when the consumer pulls a new version. It stops applying when uninstalled or disabled, and there is no mechanism to force a consumer onto a new version.
answers.failure_mode: Version skew is the standard outcome: a long tail of repos stays on an old release, so 'reaches every consumer' is aspirational unless something in CI asserts the installed version. The blast radius also cuts the other way, since one bad hook release breaks 40 repos at once, which argues for a staged rollout and a pinned-version policy rather than floating latest.
answers.version_caveat: Plugins and plugin marketplaces are among the newer extension mechanisms and shipped in a preview or experimental state at introduction, with the manifest fields and marketplace layout still settling. I cannot give the exact version or confirm whether any enabling flag is still required, so pin the Claude Code version the org supports.

answers.primary: A custom slash command holding the deploy procedure, stored under the project's commands directory so it exists only as text the harness expands when a human types its name. Pair it with a PreToolUse hook that denies the actual deploy commands unless the command run has set a marker (an env var or a short-lived file), so the procedure body is the recipe and the hook is the gate.
answers.rejected_alternative: A skill, rejected precisely because a skill is model-triggered: its description exists so the model can decide the moment has come, which is the one behaviour that must never happen here.
answers.enforcement_owner: Split, deliberately. The harness owns the trigger, since a slash command only expands on user input, and the paired hook owns the deterministic gate on the dangerous commands. The model owns the execution of the steps in between, which is why the hook is not optional.
answers.context_boundary: The command body is expanded into the current session's context at the moment it is typed, along with any arguments, and runs in that same session with full access to prior conversation. Nothing is isolated, so whatever the session already contains can influence how the steps are carried out.
answers.lifecycle: Runs only when the human types it, ends when the procedure completes or is abandoned. The marker the hook checks should be scoped to that single run so authorization does not silently persist into later turns of the same session.
answers.failure_mode: Without the hook this is advisory and fails open in the exact way the requirement forbids: nothing prevents the model from running deploy commands on its own initiative, because a command's absence does not block anything. Even with the hook, the procedure text itself can be misread, re-entered, or partially replayed, so the gate should be on the irreversible steps rather than on the command name.
answers.version_caveat: Slash commands are long-standing, but their frontmatter has grown over releases (allowed-tools, model selection, argument hints), so options available in a newer build may be ignored silently by an older one. I cannot state which version added which field.

answers.primary: A GitHub Action workflow triggered on issues: opened, running Claude Code headlessly in the runner with a prompt that labels the issue, searches open issues for likely duplicates, and posts the first-response comment through the GitHub API.
answers.rejected_alternative: A hook or a subagent inside an interactive session, rejected because both presuppose a human-opened session; the requirement is explicitly that nobody is at a terminal.
answers.enforcement_owner: Split. The harness side, meaning the workflow trigger and the token scopes, owns whether the run happens at all and what it is permitted to touch. The model owns the triage quality: the label chosen, the duplicate judgement and the tone of the comment are all unverified.
answers.context_boundary: A fresh, ephemeral context per issue event. The issue title and body, plus whatever repo state the job fetches, cross in; the label and comment API calls cross out. Nothing carries over between runs, so the bot has no memory of a similar issue triaged yesterday unless it re-queries.
answers.lifecycle: Starts on the issues-opened webhook and ends when the job exits. It stops applying when the workflow is disabled, the branch it lives on changes, or the API credential is revoked.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open and silently from the user's perspective: a failed or skipped job means the issue simply sits untriaged, and nobody notices without alerting on workflow failures. The sharper risk is that issue bodies are attacker-controlled text arriving on a public endpoint, so a crafted issue can try to steer the run; scope the token to labels and comments only, never to code or secrets, and treat the issue text as data. Cost and rate limits also scale with issue volume, including spam.
answers.version_caveat: This needs credentials in repository secrets and a supported non-interactive auth path (an API key, or a subscription-auth mechanism if the org uses one). The published Claude Code GitHub Action is versioned independently of the CLI and its input names have changed between releases, so pin the action to a tag; I cannot state which tag from model knowledge alone.

answers.primary: An agent team: five peer investigator agents launched together, each assigned one hypothesis, running against a shared task with inter-agent messaging so they can challenge each other's findings directly, plus a designated lead or a final consensus step that writes the agreed document.
answers.rejected_alternative: Five parallel subagents dispatched as Task calls, rejected because subagents are isolated: each returns a report to the orchestrator and none of them can see or rebut another's findings, so the required back-and-forth would collapse into the orchestrator summarising five monologues.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model, at every level. The harness only provides the fan-out and the message plumbing; which hypothesis survives, when the debate ends and what the consensus says are all model judgements with no deterministic check.
answers.context_boundary: Each investigator holds its own context window and its own exploration of the codebase and logs. What crosses between them is only the messages they choose to send, and what crosses back to the requesting session is the final written consensus, not the five raw investigations.
answers.lifecycle: Launched explicitly for this one investigation and ends when the consensus document is produced, a turn or budget cap is hit, or the operator stops it. It is not a standing configuration; nothing about it persists to the next bug.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory throughout. Two opposite failure shapes are common: premature convergence, where agents defer to the most confidently written argument, and non-termination, where they argue past the budget without a verdict. Because each agent argues rather than proves, a hypothesis can win on rhetoric with no evidence, so require every claim to cite a log line, stack trace or reproduction. Cost multiplies by roughly the number of agents plus the messaging overhead.
answers.version_caveat: Peer-to-peer agent teams with direct inter-agent messaging are a much newer capability than plain subagents and I believe they were still gated or evolving at the time of my knowledge cutoff. I cannot name the enabling flag, the config schema or the minimum version, and I cannot confirm whether a specific plan tier is required, so verify before designing around it; a lead-mediated pattern is the fallback if native teams are unavailable.

answers.primary: An output style, set at the project level so it applies automatically, defining the data-analyst persona and the fixed tabular reply format. An output style is the mechanism that replaces the default software-engineering system prompt rather than appending to it, which is what 'with the default engineering behavior removed' actually requires.
answers.rejected_alternative: CLAUDE.md instructions, rejected because they are additive context layered on top of the default engineering system prompt; they can ask for tables but cannot remove the behaviour underneath, so the two pull against each other on every turn.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model. The harness guarantees the style text is present in the system prompt of every turn, but adherence to the tabular format is generation behaviour with no validator, so nothing rejects a reply that drifts out of format.
answers.context_boundary: It lives in the main session's system prompt and applies to every turn of that session. It does not automatically govern subagents, which carry their own prompts, so any delegated work can come back in the default voice unless those agents are configured to match.
answers.lifecycle: Applies from the moment it is selected, persists across sessions in the project once written into project settings, and stops when it is switched back or overridden by a user-level setting. It governs interactive turns; headless or scripted invocations may not pick it up.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory and fails open. Format drift grows with session length and with awkward inputs that do not fit the table columns, and the model will sometimes break format to report an error. The bigger operational risk is over-removal: stripping engineering behaviour also strips the instincts needed when the annotation project genuinely requires a script or a file edit, so define the escape hatch explicitly in the style.
answers.version_caveat: Output styles were introduced after the initial Claude Code releases and the surrounding configuration has been in flux; I am not confident about the current settings key name or whether the mechanism has since been folded into another one, so confirm against the installed version before committing the project setting.

answers.primary: A headless CLI invocation in the CI job (claude -p, or the Agent SDK driven from a script) run with explicit isolation: a pinned dated model id, a settings file checked into the repo passed explicitly, and MCP configuration restricted to exactly what is passed on the command line rather than discovered. The run must not inherit user-level settings from whoever's machine or runner image it lands on.
answers.rejected_alternative: A GitHub Action left on its defaults, rejected not because CI is wrong but because a default-configured run still discovers the repo's MCP config and any settings present in the environment, which is the exact leakage the requirement names.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Which configuration sources load is decided by the CLI flags and the process environment, not by the model, so isolation is enforceable even though the output text is not.
answers.context_boundary: A fresh process and a fresh context per pull request. The diff and the fixed prompt cross in; the typo and lint findings cross out, ideally as structured output the job parses. Nothing from a developer's home directory, personal hooks, personal subagents or the project's tool-server file should cross in at all, and that is the property the flags exist to guarantee.
answers.lifecycle: Runs once per pull request event and terminates with the job. It stops applying when the CI step is removed; it holds no state between runs, which is itself part of the reproducibility argument.
answers.failure_mode: The configuration isolation fails open and silently: omit the strict-config flag and the extra sources merge in with no error, producing a run that looks fine and is not reproducible. More fundamentally, byte-for-byte identical output is not achievable from a language model even with identical inputs, since sampling is not guaranteed deterministic and the served model can change beneath a floating alias. Treat 'same config, same pinned model, same input' as the achievable guarantee and assert on the findings set rather than on the exact bytes.
answers.version_caveat: The flags that control config sources (a strict MCP config flag, an explicit settings path, and controls over which setting sources load) have been added and renamed across releases, so I will not assert exact spellings from memory; check --help on the pinned CLI version. Pin both the Claude Code version and a dated model identifier rather than a latest-style alias, since alias resolution alone will break run-to-run stability.
